messages.content: I need to design recoverable distributed snapshots for migrating stream operators, with reordered messages and concurrent worker failures. Recovery must preserve a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash. The design also needs to maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput without globally pausing processing. How should I read these constraints together?

They impose separate correctness and performance requirements on the same design. A recoverable snapshot must give recovery a coherent distributed state even when operators migrate and messages arrive out of order. After any single worker crash, recovery must preserve a consistent cut and avoid both missing and duplicate outputs. At the same time, snapshotting must retain at least 85% of the throughput achieved with snapshots disabled, without stopping processing across the whole system to make a snapshot.
What makes the cut consistent if different workers observe events at different times?

A consistent cut is not necessarily a single instant that every worker observes simultaneously. Conceptually, it is a selection of local histories that can belong to one coherent distributed history. In particular, it cannot include a message’s receipt while excluding the send on which that receipt depends. It may include a send without the corresponding receipt, provided recovery can account for that message as still in transit. The requirement is about that causal coherence, not identical wall-clock snapshot times.
Does message reordering change that definition?

The definition of a consistent cut stays the same, but reordering makes it unsafe to infer causality or completeness from arrival order alone. Receiving one message does not, by itself, establish that every message sent earlier along a path has already arrived. Whatever state the snapshot represents must remain coherent despite that possibility; the task does not prescribe a particular way to represent or track the messages.
And how does migration enter the snapshot problem?

Migration means an operator can move while the system is processing messages and taking snapshots. The recoverable view must remain coherent across that movement: it cannot treat work as absent merely because it was between locations, or count the same work twice because both locations appear in a snapshot. That describes the consistency obligation, not a specified migration procedure or a decision about how snapshots are taken.
So a snapshot of every worker’s local operator state would not automatically be enough?

Not automatically. Local states are part of a distributed cut, but their combination also has to respect interactions between workers, including messages that were sent, received, or still in transit. Migration adds another boundary across which work may be in progress. A collection of individually valid local states is recoverable only if, together with whatever else recovery needs to know, it represents a consistent cut.
Is a consistent cut sufficient to get exactly-once outputs?

No. A consistent cut addresses whether the recovered distributed state is coherent. Exactly-once outputs additionally concern what an observer sees across a crash and recovery: an output must not disappear, and an output already produced must not appear a second time because work is repeated. The two requirements have to hold together, but satisfying one does not by itself prove the other.
Does exactly-once mean that no internal computation can ever run twice?

The stated requirement is exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash, not an assertion that each internal step executes exactly once. Recovery may need to revisit work; the externally observable output must still meet the exactly-once requirement. That distinction matters when assessing a design, without specifying which recovery mechanism it uses.
What if the single worker crashes during a migration or while a snapshot is being taken?

The single-worker-crash guarantee is stated without an exception for those moments. A design should therefore be assessed against a crash occurring while migration or snapshot activity is in progress, as well as at other times. It still has to recover to a consistent cut and preserve exactly-once outputs. Nothing in the goal specifies how an incomplete migration or snapshot is represented or resolved.
The goal also mentions concurrent worker failures. Does that mean the same guarantee applies after several workers crash together?

Concurrent worker failures are part of the design problem, but the explicit recovery guarantee is phrased as applying after any single worker crash. It would overstate the requirement to claim that the same guarantee has been specified for every multi-worker crash. Conversely, the mention of concurrent failures should not be silently discarded; their role needs to be kept in view without inventing a stronger stated guarantee.
Could the system make a consistent snapshot simply by pausing all processing until it is complete?

That would conflict with the explicit condition against globally pausing processing. The requirement leaves room for coordination, but not for a system-wide processing stop as the way to obtain snapshots. The design has to meet its correctness conditions while processing continues rather than relying on a global pause to make every worker line up.
Does ‘without globally pausing’ prohibit every brief wait by an individual worker?

No such blanket prohibition is stated. The condition rules out globally pausing processing; it does not say that no component may ever wait or coordinate. Any such behavior would still have to be compatible with the at-least-85% throughput requirement. The node does not specify a permitted coordination technique or a separate limit on local waits.
How should I interpret the 85% figure precisely?

It is a relative throughput floor: with the snapshot design in use, throughput must be at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput. Equivalently, the permitted drop relative to that baseline is no more than 15% of baseline throughput. It is not an absolute records-per-second target, and it is not permission to meet the number by globally pausing processing. No workload, measurement interval, or measured throughput is supplied here.
If throughput meets that threshold but recovery duplicates an output, would the design satisfy the goal?

No. The throughput threshold does not relax the recovery requirement. After any single worker crash, recovery must preserve a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs. Conversely, a design that achieves those recovery properties but falls below 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput, or relies on a global processing pause, would not meet all the stated requirements.
What is the core tension tying all of this together?

The snapshot must describe a coherent point in distributed execution even though messages can be reordered, operators can migrate, and worker failures can occur concurrently with other activity. Recovery after any single worker crash must use that coherent view without losing or duplicating outputs. Obtaining and maintaining it cannot depend on halting all processing, and its throughput cost must leave at least 85% of the snapshot-disabled baseline. Those are the constraints to satisfy; they do not, on their own, select an implementation.
Then the right question is not just whether each worker saves a state, but whether the saved view and the outputs remain coherent across message delivery, migration, and a single crash?

Yes. The saved view must form a recoverable, consistent distributed cut, and the outputs observed across recovery from any single worker crash must be exactly once. Reordered messages and operator migration are conditions under which that has to work, while concurrent worker failures remain part of the broader design problem. The design must also maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput without globally pausing processing.
I propose using asynchronous epoch snapshots with per-channel sequence fences, durable in-flight logs, fenced migration handoffs, and transactional sink commits. How do those pieces fit together?

They address different boundaries in the same recovery problem. Epoch snapshots organize the distributed state into recoverable snapshot rounds without requiring a global processing pause. Per-channel sequence fences help define which messages belong on each side of a snapshot boundary, even when arrival order is misleading. Durable in-flight logs account for messages that have crossed a send boundary but are not yet reflected in a receiving operator’s saved state. Fenced migration handoffs address which location may act for a migrating operator. Transactional sink commits address when outputs become externally visible. Together, these are a proposed approach, not yet a demonstration that the recovery and throughput requirements are met.
What does an epoch contribute beyond saying ‘take a snapshot’?

An epoch provides a way to refer to the same logical snapshot round across distributed components. That matters because their local states need not be captured at one wall-clock instant: the design needs to establish which states and messages collectively belong to a coherent cut. An epoch label alone does not establish that coherence; the message boundaries, in-flight information, migration handoffs, and output commits must agree with it.
Does ‘asynchronous’ mean the workers take snapshots independently with no coordination?

Not necessarily. Here, asynchronous means the proposal does not depend on globally pausing processing while a snapshot is made. Establishing a coherent distributed cut can still require coordination or agreed boundaries. The proposal does not specify a detailed protocol or claim that every worker proceeds without ever waiting.
Why are the sequence fences per channel rather than just one marker for the whole system?

A consistent cut has to account for messages on the communication paths between components. A per-channel sequence fence describes a boundary for a particular channel, so the design can reason about messages on that channel rather than treating all arrivals as one ordered stream. That is especially relevant when messages may be reordered: a message’s arrival position alone cannot settle which side of the boundary other messages belong on. The proposal does not specify the sequence-numbering or fence protocol.
If a later message arrives before an earlier one, should the later arrival move the snapshot boundary?

It should not be assumed to do so merely because it arrived first. The point of sequence fences is to make the boundary meaningful independently of that arrival-order shortcut. The design would need to identify which messages are included in the saved receiver state and which remain to be accounted for as in flight. This proposal names the mechanism at a high level; it does not give a rule for processing every reordered arrival.
Where do the durable in-flight logs come in?

They address the gap between saved states when a message has been sent on one side of the cut but has not been incorporated into the saved receiving state. Such a message can be consistent with the cut, but recovery must not simply forget it. A durable in-flight log is the proposed means of retaining the information needed to account for messages in that gap. Its durability matters because a worker crash must not erase the only recoverable record of relevant in-flight work.
Would logging every message automatically give us a consistent cut?

No. Logging and cut consistency are different questions. The saved local states, the channel boundaries, and the logged in-flight messages still have to fit together: for example, recovery cannot include a receipt while excluding the send it depends on. Nor should it both recover a message as in flight and treat its effects as already incorporated without accounting for that overlap. The proposal has to make those relationships precise before its correctness can be established.
How does a fenced handoff help when an operator migrates?

It proposes an explicit boundary around the change of location, so the snapshot and recovery logic can distinguish responsibility before and after the handoff. The purpose of fencing is to prevent ambiguous authority over a migrating operator from turning into lost work or duplicated work. That is the role of the mechanism; the proposal does not specify a particular ownership token, transfer sequence, or failure-resolution procedure.
Can an epoch snapshot span a migration?

The proposal needs to remain coherent when snapshot activity and migration overlap. In that situation, the epoch’s saved states and message accounting would have to agree with the fenced handoff: they cannot leave the operator’s work unrepresented between locations or treat both locations as independently entitled to produce the same output. Whether a particular implementation permits a handoff at a particular point in an epoch is not specified here.
Is the migration fence the same thing as a per-channel sequence fence?

They serve related but distinct purposes. A per-channel sequence fence establishes a message boundary on a channel. A fenced migration handoff establishes a boundary around responsibility for an operator as it moves. Both must be compatible with the epoch’s recoverable cut, but a message boundary by itself does not settle who may act for the operator, and a migration handoff by itself does not account for every in-flight message.
What role do transactional sink commits play if the snapshots already cover operator state?

Recovering coherent operator state does not, by itself, settle what has already become visible outside the operators. Transactional sink commits are the proposed way to coordinate output visibility with recoverable progress, so replay after a single worker crash does not make an already visible output appear a second time or leave an intended output missing. The proposal does not specify a transaction protocol or establish, merely by naming transactional commits, that exactly-once outputs have been proved.
So the sink transaction boundary has to agree with the snapshot epoch?

Yes, in the sense that recovered state and visible output must tell a compatible story. If recovery returns to a saved cut, it must not treat outputs as uncommitted work when they are already visible in a way that would cause duplicates; nor can it assume an output is safely visible if it is not. Epoch snapshots and transactional sink commits are proposed as parts of that coordination, without a specified commit order or detailed protocol.
What would I need to check for a crash that happens while one of these boundaries is changing?

The relevant check is whether recovery can still identify a consistent cut and exactly-once output history after any single worker crash, including one during snapshot activity or an operator handoff. That means examining whether saved state, channel fences, durable in-flight information, handoff responsibility, and sink visibility remain mutually compatible. The proposal identifies those elements but does not yet supply a proof for every crash point.
And the mention of concurrent worker failures—do these components imply a guarantee for multiple workers crashing together?

Not by themselves. The broader design problem includes concurrent worker failures, while the explicit recovery requirement says ‘after any single worker crash.’ Durable logs and fencing are relevant to failures, but this proposal does not establish a particular guarantee for simultaneous crashes of multiple workers. That distinction should remain clear when describing what has and has not been shown.
Does this approach meet the at-least-85% throughput target because it avoids a global pause?

Avoiding a global pause addresses one condition, but it does not prove the throughput condition. Sequence fences, durable logging, handoffs, snapshot work, and sink transactions can all have costs. The proposed design would still need to maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput; no measurement or performance result is given here. ‘Asynchronous’ describes the intended processing behavior, not an established throughput figure.
Is it fair to describe the proposal as separating state, messages, migration responsibility, and output visibility without claiming those concerns are independent?

Yes. Epoch snapshots organize saved state; per-channel sequence fences and durable in-flight logs address message boundaries and messages between saved states; fenced handoffs address migrating-operator responsibility; and transactional sink commits address output visibility. They are distinct concerns, but the recovery guarantee depends on their boundaries agreeing. The proposal is to use all of them together while continuing processing, subject to proving consistent-cut and exactly-once recovery after any single worker crash and meeting the 85%-of-snapshot-disabled-throughput floor.
Then I should present these as proposed mechanisms, not as evidence that the correctness and performance targets have already been reached?

Exactly. State the proposed combination explicitly, and distinguish what each mechanism is meant to handle from a verified outcome. In particular, neither a consistent cut, exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash, nor at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput follows solely from listing the mechanisms.
How can per-channel cuts remain consistent when reordered records cross migration handoffs and a worker crashes mid-commit?

The key is to make three boundaries agree without assuming that arrival order defines any of them: each channel’s snapshot boundary, the handoff of responsibility for the migrating operator, and the boundary at which outputs become committed. A coherent recovery must be able to place each relevant record in saved operator state or account for it as in flight, without losing it or applying it twice. If the worker crashes during a sink commit, recovery must also determine how the output’s visibility relates to that recoverable state. The proposed fences, durable in-flight logs, and transactional sink commits are intended to address those obligations, but the question exposes details that the proposal has not yet specified.
Why is arrival order especially dangerous at the handoff?

A record that arrives at one location later is not necessarily later in the channel’s sequence. If responsibility for the operator changes while records are being reordered, observing a record on one side of the handoff cannot establish that all preceding records were observed there too. The channel cut therefore needs a meaning independent of which location happened to see a record first. The handoff must also leave no ambiguity about which location’s state or recoverable in-flight information accounts for that record.
Could I simply treat everything received by the old worker as pre-handoff and everything received by the new worker as post-handoff?

Not safely on receipt location alone. Reordering means records associated with an earlier channel boundary might arrive after the handoff, and migration means the place that receives a record need not, by itself, establish how it belongs in the recoverable operator history. You would have to show that the proposed classification still accounts for every record consistently with the per-channel cut and with the fenced transfer of responsibility. The question does not supply such a rule.
Then what exactly does the per-channel sequence fence need to tell recovery?

At the conceptual level, it must identify the channel boundary used by the snapshot: which records are represented in the receiving state and which records still need to be accounted for across that boundary. A later arrival must not silently stand in for an earlier record that is still missing. The fence only does its job if its interpretation remains compatible with the saved states, the durable in-flight log, and the migration handoff. A sequence fence by itself is not a complete recovery rule.
Can different channels have different boundaries and still form one cut?

Yes, a distributed cut need not place every channel at the same apparent instant or sequence position. Its boundaries must jointly be causally consistent: recovery cannot include a record’s receipt while excluding the send on which that receipt depends. A send without a saved receipt can fit the cut if the corresponding in-flight record remains recoverable. Reordering makes careful accounting important, but does not require all channels to have identical boundaries.
What does it mean for a reordered record to ‘cross’ the migration handoff?

It means the record’s relevant channel position and the change in operator responsibility cannot be inferred from a simple before-or-after arrival at one worker. A record may be in transit while responsibility moves, or arrive in an order that makes its place relative to the fence unclear from observation alone. The design has to establish whether its effect is already in saved state or whether the record remains recoverable for processing under the appropriate responsibility. ‘Crossing’ the handoff must not make it vanish or allow both sides to count its effect.
Would the durable in-flight log resolve that ambiguity automatically?

It can preserve information about records that are not yet represented in the saved receiving state, including ones affected by reordering or a handoff. But durability alone does not resolve whether a particular record has already affected saved state or output. The log, per-channel fence, and handoff boundary need compatible interpretations so that recovery neither omits the record nor replays an effect that is already accounted for.
Is the handoff fence primarily about where the state is stored?

Its central purpose here is to make responsibility for the migrating operator unambiguous across the handoff. Where state is stored matters to recoverability, but a copy of state at two locations would not, by itself, settle which location may act on records or produce outputs. The handoff boundary must be compatible with what the channel cuts say about pending records. No particular transfer procedure or form of fencing is specified.
Suppose a record is not included in the old worker’s saved operator state and has not yet affected the new worker’s saved state. Is that necessarily an inconsistent cut?

Not necessarily. A consistent cut can leave a sent record in flight rather than include its receipt. In the proposed approach, recovery would need durable information sufficient to account for that record, and the handoff would need to identify responsibility for it. It would be a problem if the record were absent from both saved state and recoverable in-flight information, or if its effect were counted in both places without a way to avoid duplication.
What if a later-sequenced record has already been processed when that earlier one turns up?

That is precisely why the cut cannot be defined as ‘everything up to the most recently arrived record.’ The design must be able to explain both records’ positions relative to the channel fence and what effects, if any, are already represented in saved state. This question does not prescribe whether processing waits, proceeds, or uses another technique when records arrive out of order. Whichever behavior is chosen would have to preserve a consistent recoverable cut.
Now add the worker crash mid-commit. What uncertainty does that create?

A worker may fail without recovery being able to infer from its last local action alone whether an output became externally committed. If recovery assumes the output did not commit when it did, repeating the output risks a duplicate. If recovery assumes it did commit when it did not, the output risks being lost. Transactional sink commits are proposed to make output visibility recoverable and compatible with the saved cut, but the proposal has not specified how an uncertain commit outcome is determined.
So it is not enough for the channel cut and handoff to agree if sink visibility disagrees?

Correct. They could describe a coherent internal history while the external output history still violates exactly-once behavior. For recovery after any single worker crash, the state it restores, the records it accounts for or reprocesses, and the outputs the sink has committed must form a compatible account. A mid-commit crash tests that compatibility at a particularly awkward point.
If the output really was committed before the crash, can recovery still revisit its input record?

Revisiting internal work is not itself forbidden by the exactly-once-outputs requirement. The issue is whether revisiting it makes the already committed output visible again. Transactional sink commits are part of the proposed answer, but a correctness argument would have to show how the committed outcome stays associated with the recovered work even when the worker crashed mid-commit. This is a condition the design must satisfy, not an outcome established by the proposal alone.
And if the commit had not actually happened?

Then recovery must not treat the output as safely produced and leave it missing. It must be possible to complete the intended output consistently with the recovered state and record accounting, without turning any already committed output into a duplicate. The two possible commit outcomes illustrate why merely knowing that a worker started a commit is insufficient.
Do the channel fence and migration fence have to advance together with a sink commit?

The requirement is compatibility among their recoverable boundaries, not necessarily that they change at the same wall-clock instant. A design could only claim correctness if, for every relevant crash point, it can explain which channel records are in the cut, where operator responsibility lies, and which outputs are committed. The proposed mechanisms do not specify an ordering among those operations, so assuming a particular sequence would go beyond the proposal.
How would I frame the consistency check without claiming a protocol we have not defined?

Frame it as a set of questions about each recoverable state. Can every received record in the cut be traced to a send in the cut? Are sent but not yet incorporated records still recoverable? Does the fenced handoff leave one coherent account of the migrating operator’s responsibility and effects? If a worker crashes mid-commit, can recovery reconcile the actual sink outcome with replay so that outputs appear exactly once? Those checks express what the design must establish without assuming how its mechanisms are implemented.
Does checking a mid-commit worker crash also answer what happens when multiple workers fail at once?

No. It addresses one crash point under the explicit requirement for recovery after any single worker crash. Concurrent worker failures are part of the broader design problem, but neither this question nor the proposed mechanisms establish a particular recovery guarantee for a simultaneous multi-worker crash. A claim about that case would require its own stated conditions and reasoning.
Is there a temptation to solve the ordering issue by stopping all workers at the handoff?

A global processing pause would conflict with the stated constraint. The asynchronous snapshot proposal is meant to work without one, while using boundaries and recoverable in-flight information to reason about work in progress. Even if those mechanisms establish correctness, the design would still need to maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput; neither the absence of a global pause nor this consistency argument establishes that performance result.
So the hard case is not just a record arriving out of order, but recovering one coherent story about that record, the handoff, and the output commit after the worker disappears?

Exactly. The record’s place relative to its per-channel cut must not depend solely on arrival order; the fenced migration handoff must make its operator-side responsibility and effects unambiguous; and a mid-commit crash must not leave output visibility ambiguous in a way that causes loss or duplication. Durable in-flight logs and transactional sink commits are proposed to help maintain that coherent story. Whether the particular design achieves it remains to be specified and demonstrated.

My hypothesis is that durable contiguous-sequence fences and ownership epochs should preserve consistent cuts and exactly-once sink commits despite reordering and mid-handoff crashes. Is that a fair way to state it?

Yes, as a hypothesis rather than an established guarantee. The contiguous-sequence fences are meant to keep a reordered arrival from making a channel boundary appear further along than the records that have actually been accounted for. Ownership epochs are meant to make responsibility for a migrating operator distinguishable across a handoff. The hypothesis is that, together with the proposed recoverable message and sink accounting, those boundaries will support consistent cuts and exactly-once sink commits even if a worker crashes during the handoff. That still needs a precise correctness argument.
What does ‘contiguous’ add to a sequence fence?

It distinguishes a complete prefix from merely the highest sequence position observed. If one record arrives ahead of an earlier one, seeing the later position cannot establish that the earlier position has been accounted for. A contiguous-sequence fence is intended to mark a boundary with no unexplained gap before it. That does not require every record beyond the fence to be discarded; it means their relationship to the saved state and recoverable in-flight information must be explicit.
When you say ‘accounted for,’ do you mean already processed by the operator?

Not necessarily. For a recoverable cut, a record can be accounted for in saved operator state or as a recoverable in-flight record, depending on where the cut places it. The important point is not to mistake a later arrival for proof that an earlier record has safely become part of saved state. The hypothesis would need to define exactly what advancing a particular fence certifies; the word ‘contiguous’ alone does not settle that.
Could a later record be observed while the contiguous fence stays behind it?

Conceptually, yes. Reordering is precisely the case in which an observed high sequence position and a complete prefix can differ. The fence should not advance across an unexplained gap simply because a later record appeared. A design would still have to specify how that later record is represented in the recoverable view; this hypothesis does not choose a processing or storage procedure for it.
Why specify that the fence is durable?

If the boundary exists only in the memory of a worker that crashes, recovery cannot reliably use it to distinguish what the snapshot includes from what still needs accounting. Durability is intended to make the boundary recoverable across that crash. It does not by itself prove that the boundary is correct or that every record near it is durable; the fence has to agree with the saved state and any relevant in-flight log.
Is a durable fence enough to make an in-flight record recoverable?

No. A fence identifies a boundary; it is not automatically a copy of every record on either side. The proposed durable in-flight logs address records that a consistent cut leaves between sent and incorporated states. For the hypothesis to hold, the fence and those recoverable records must give a compatible account, including when arrival order differs from sequence order.
How does an ownership epoch differ from the snapshot epoch?

They label different concepts. A snapshot epoch identifies a recoverable snapshot round. An ownership epoch, in this hypothesis, distinguishes responsibility for a migrating operator across handoffs. They need to be compatible when recovery combines operator state, channel boundaries, and output visibility, but sharing the word ‘epoch’ does not make them the same boundary or require them to advance together.
What would ownership epochs prevent during a handoff?

Their intended role is to keep responsibility from being ambiguous when the operator moves. A crash mid-handoff should not leave recovery treating work as ownerless, nor treating two locations as independently authorized to count the same effects. The hypothesis is that distinguishing ownership epochs can support that separation. It does not yet specify how authority changes hands or how a partially completed handoff is resolved.
Could the channel fence advance under one owner while a reordered record appears to another?

That is a case the hypothesis must be able to explain. Arrival at a location cannot, on its own, determine whether a record falls before or after the channel’s contiguous boundary, or which ownership epoch is responsible for its effect. Recovery needs one coherent account of the record: whether its effect is already represented in saved state or it remains recoverable as in flight, and which ownership epoch may act on it. The hypothesis proposes boundaries for that reasoning, not a completed rule for the case.
If a worker crashes partway through the handoff, must recovery always choose the old owner?

The hypothesis does not specify that choice. It calls for ownership epochs to make the recoverable responsibility unambiguous despite a mid-handoff crash. Depending on the boundary actually established, a sound design would have to explain which responsibility is recoverable without losing or duplicating work. Assuming that the old or the new owner always wins would add a handoff rule that has not been supplied.
So I should not equate ‘the new worker has seen a record’ with ‘ownership has transferred’?

Right. Observation of a record, completion of a contiguous channel prefix, and transfer of operator responsibility are distinct facts. Reordering can separate observation from sequence position; a mid-handoff crash can make an incomplete transfer especially important. The proposed ownership epochs are meant to let recovery identify responsibility independently of that simple observation.
Where does the consistent-cut claim come from, if the two kinds of epoch are different?

It would come from showing that their boundaries can be combined into a causally coherent saved history. For each channel, a received record included in the cut must have its sending side included; a sent record not yet incorporated at the receiver must remain accounted for. Across migration, the operator effects represented in saved state and the responsibility indicated by ownership epochs must not leave a gap or count the same effect twice. The hypothesis says the durable contiguous-sequence fences and ownership epochs should make that possible; their existence alone is not the proof.
What does ‘exactly-once sink commits’ add beyond that consistent cut?

It adds a requirement about externally visible outputs. A coherent internal cut does not prevent recovery from committing an output again if it was already committed, or from omitting one that was not committed. The hypothesis therefore has to connect the recoverable channel and ownership boundaries to the transactional sink commits in the proposal. Its intended result is that sink-visible outputs remain exactly once despite reordering and a crash mid-handoff.
Does an ownership epoch alone tell us whether a sink commit happened?

No. It can distinguish responsibility for the operator, but it is not itself evidence of an output’s committed state at the sink. The correctness argument would need compatible recoverable information about output visibility as well. Otherwise, knowing which owner should act would not settle whether repeating an output would duplicate it or withholding it would lose it.
Could two ownership epochs both appear in a snapshot without making the cut inconsistent?

Their appearance alone would not decide consistency. A distributed cut can include a handoff boundary and state from different participants; what matters is whether the combined history has a coherent account of responsibility and effects. It must not grant conflicting authority to produce the same output, and it must still account for records that cross the handoff. The hypothesis would need to establish those properties rather than rely on the epoch labels by themselves.
What if an earlier-sequenced record is still missing when the operator moves?

Then a contiguous-sequence fence should not treat that missing position as settled merely because later records arrived. The recoverable cut must still account for the earlier record according to whether it has been sent, incorporated into saved state, or remains in flight. Ownership epochs must also leave a coherent responsibility for handling it after the handoff. This is an important case for the hypothesis, but it does not specify a procedure for moving or processing the record.
Does the hypothesis promise that a crash mid-handoff cannot lose any record?

That is part of what preserving a recoverable consistent cut would require, provided the record belongs to the recoverable distributed history being considered. The statement is a prediction that the proposed boundaries should achieve that property, not a report that every crash point has been checked. In particular, a durable fence cannot substitute for durable in-flight information where the cut needs it.
What about the earlier question of a worker crashing mid-commit rather than mid-handoff?

It remains an important case for exactly-once outputs, but this hypothesis specifically names reordering and mid-handoff crashes. It should not be stretched into a proved account of every mid-commit outcome. To establish the broader single-worker-crash requirement, the design would also need to show that recovery can reconcile the sink’s actual commit outcome with the recovered state when a crash occurs during a commit.
And does ‘should preserve’ mean we can claim the single-worker recovery requirement is met?

No. ‘Should’ marks this as a hypothesis about how the mechanisms might satisfy that requirement. A claim that recovery preserves a consistent cut and exactly-once outputs after any single worker crash would require showing that the boundaries and sink outcomes remain compatible at the relevant crash points. The hypothesis identifies a plausible basis for that argument; it is not the completed argument.
Does it say anything definite about simultaneous crashes of several workers?

No. Concurrent worker failures remain part of the design problem, but the hypothesis does not state a multi-worker recovery guarantee. Its reference to mid-handoff crashes should not be read as proving what happens for every combination of simultaneous worker failures.
Could these durable boundaries impose enough overhead to violate the throughput target?

They could impose overhead; the hypothesis supplies no measurement either way. The design still needs to maintain at least 85% of snapshot-disabled throughput without globally pausing processing. Correctness under reordering and mid-handoff crashes would not establish that separate performance condition, and meeting the throughput floor would not establish correctness.
How can I express what remains to be demonstrated without turning the hypothesis into an implementation plan?

You can state the obligations rather than choose procedures: show that contiguous fences never conceal an unaccounted-for gap; that saved state and durable in-flight information agree with those fences; that ownership epochs give one coherent account of operator responsibility across a crashed handoff; and that recovered work agrees with what the sink has committed, so outputs are exactly once. Those are tests of the hypothesis’s meaning, not claims that a particular protocol or result already exists.
Then the claim is deliberately narrower than saying the labels alone solve the problem?

Yes. The hypothesis is that *durable contiguous-sequence fences and ownership epochs should help preserve* consistent cuts and exactly-once sink commits despite reordering and mid-handoff crashes. It depends on those boundaries being interpreted compatibly with recoverable records, operator state, and transactional output visibility. Merely attaching sequence numbers and epoch labels would not, by itself, establish the claim.

I want to specify contiguous-sequence cuts and durable ownership epochs, crash-inject reordered handoffs, and then audit the recovered cuts and sink duplicates. How should I describe that plan without making it sound like a result?

Describe it as a sequence of work to be done: first define what the channel cuts and ownership epochs mean, then inject crashes during handoffs involving reordered records, and afterward inspect the recovered cuts and sink outputs for duplicates. That describes what must be unambiguous; it does not prescribe a particular numbering or storage procedure.

Without a defined cut, an audit would have no clear standard for deciding whether recovered state and in-flight records form a coherent history. Specifying the boundary first gives the later audit a meaning to check, rather than letting the observed recovery behavior define consistency after the fact.

It should identify how responsibility for a migrating operator is distinguished across a handoff in recoverable information. ‘Durable’ matters because the worker participating in a handoff may crash; recovery must not depend solely on its lost local memory to interpret responsibility. The plan calls for specifying that boundary, not for assuming that an epoch label by itself prevents conflicting ownership.

No. The contiguous-sequence cut concerns which channel records are represented at a snapshot boundary. The ownership epoch concerns responsibility for the operator across migration. The relevant condition is that record arrival order does not reliably indicate sequence position while responsibility is moving between workers.
